rationale: PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence for the broad target trait arthritis: it reports clean PGS-only metrics (AUROC 0.539 and PGS-only R² 0.00291) with basic covariates and these are sanity-consistent with the provided low heritability ceiling guidance, whereas PGS004547 provides no AUROC/R² at all (only an OR=1.262, which is weak-to-moderate) and has unknown covariates. Although PGS004547 uses a more complex/meta-PRS method and far more variants, its endpoint is a narrower/administrative subtype label (“M13 Other arthritis”) and the lack of comparable performance metrics makes it less well evidenced than PGS001135’s directly comparable PRS-only evaluation.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on structural and effect-size evidence. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with far broader variant coverage (326,000 vs 858) and shows a slightly stronger reported discrimination via OR(top 10% vs rest)=1.96 (1.54–2.51) vs 1.76 (1.32–2.34) for PGS002739. PGS002739 is constrained to AFR evaluation only and uses a gene-based sparse score, which is a weaker structural signal for a polygenic disorder absent clearly superior metrics. Therefore PGS002738 is better supported overall, though confidence is tempered because both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and covariates are unknown.

PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait aortic stenosis because its concept alignment is direct (trait_reported and trait_efo both aortic stenosis), whereas PGS005255 is primarily labeled as a hemodynamic measurement (trait_reported: Mean pressure gradient; trait_efo includes aortic measurement), making it less endpoint-faithful on the visible metadata despite sharing the same phenotyping_reported (incident aortic stenosis). Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same paper, PRS-CS, EUR-only dev/eval, same validation N and covariates, no PRS-only AUC/R2), so the tie-breakers are endpoint fidelity and available effect-size strength; PGS005254 also shows a slightly stronger HR per SD (1.64 vs 1.53).

PGS001267 and PGS001268 are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper (same training n=269,704, same 10 variants, same covariates, same ancestry distribution, same validation n=67,425), so the main differentiator is endpoint fidelity. For a generic target trait of ankylosing spondylitis, PGS001267 uses a direct disease endpoint (phenotyping_reported/trait_reported: ankylosing spondylitis), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly time-to-event (TTE) / incident-style packaging, which is a mild mismatch for generic disease risk. Although PGS001268 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.7346/0.1023 vs 0.7265/0.0988), the metric gap is small and both are well below the heritability ceiling; the cleaner endpoint match in PGS001267 is the deciding factor.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis), but PGS004913 has cleaner endpoint fidelity in phenotyping_reported (Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis) whereas PGS001777’s phenotyping_reported is restricted/shifted (Cirrhosis (males)). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so PGS001777’s full-model AUROC=0.671 cannot be treated as standalone PRS evidence; in contrast PGS004913 provides a PRS-comparable signal via an R²=0.029 and an OR top vs bottom deciles=4.4. PGS004913 also has explicit basic covariates (age, sex, 10 PCs) and larger, multi-cohort disease-focused development/validation (training n=3,037; validation n=3,360) versus PGS001777’s unknown covariates and smaller validation (n=1,390). Overall, PGS004913 is better-supported on endpoint clarity and comparable performance evidence.

PGS001135 is better supported on the visible fields: it provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.539 and PGS-only R²=0.00291) with basic covariates and a heritability-sane signal (well below the arthritis h2_liability ceiling). It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) even though the selected record is EUR. In contrast, PGS004477 has a more specific reported endpoint label (“M13 Other arthritis”) and a genome-wide LDpred2 build with many variants, but it reports no PRS-only AUC/R² (only an OR=1.20, which is weak-to-moderate) and has unknown covariates, making its predictive evidence and comparability materially less clear despite larger validation N.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) at the trait_reported/trait_efo level, but PGS003972 has stronger structural and study-support signals: it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1.1M variants developed in a large multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis context (many contributing cohorts listed), whereas PGS000753 is a sparse P+T score with only 29 variants from a more limited development context. Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC=0.69 reported for PGS003972 cannot be used as a PRS-comparable advantage; however, PGS000753’s only comparable performance evidence is a moderate OR=1.37 per SD, which does not outweigh the much stronger methodological properties and broader disease-focused consortium-style support visible for PGS003972. Covariates are basic/known for PGS000753 but unknown for PGS003972, lowering confidence somewhat, yet there is no explicit clinical-risk packaging or biomarker leakage shown for either.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper, with identical training cohort (UKB), training N (269,704), covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size (24,905), so endpoint/transportability evidence is essentially tied. Candidate_a (PGS001261) has slightly better PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.58233 vs 0.58108; PGS-only R2 0.01228 vs 0.01185; incremental AUROC 0.00796 vs 0.00783), and its phenotyping is explicitly time-to-event angina pectoris (still aligned to angina pectoris) while candidate_b is a more generic 'Angina'. The metric differences are tiny and both R2 values are plausible under the heritability ceiling, hence low confidence, but PGS001261 has the marginally stronger quantitative support.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper, with identical trait_efo (angina pectoris), similar basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), and the same DEV/EVAL ancestry pattern, so endpoint fidelity and study archetype do not differentiate much (PGS001262 uses the explicit doctor-diagnosed UKB field; PGS001260 is labeled more generically as Angina). On PRS-comparable metrics, PGS001262 is modestly stronger: higher PGS-only AUROC (0.5868 vs 0.5811) and higher PGS-only R² (0.01304 vs 0.01185), with both remaining plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling. PGS001260 has larger training N and more variants, but those are weaker signals here and do not outweigh the consistently better PRS-only performance in PGS001262.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to ankylosing spondylitis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array etc.), so phenotype fidelity and leakage risk are essentially tied. PGS001267 is better supported on directly PRS-comparable performance: it reports PRS-only AUROC=0.7265 and PRS-only R²=0.0988 in Europeans, with CIs for AUROC, enabling clean comparison; these values are also plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling guidance (not obviously exceeding it). PGS002089 lacks PRS-only AUC/R² and only provides a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919), which is weaker and less standard as a PRS performance summary. Although PGS002089 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with many variants and includes some non-EUR evaluation, the absence of comparable PRS-only metrics makes its empirical support thinner than PGS001267’s.

PGS002089 has the cleaner endpoint match to the target trait (phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are simply “Ankylosing spondylitis”), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) formulation (“Ankylosing spondylitis (time-to-event)”, “TTE ankylosing spondylitis”), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease-risk target. Although PGS001268 reports explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.7346; PGS-only R2 0.10232) and PGS002089 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial-r 0.0919), PGS001268 comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 10-variant model (snpnet), a known generalization risk signal versus genome-wide shrinkage. PGS002089 uses LDpred2 with far broader genome-wide coverage (22,026 variants) and is evaluated across multiple non-EUR groups (EUR/GME/SAS), which supports portability. Net: better phenotype fidelity + stronger structural method/coverage favors PGS002089, but confidence is low because PGS001268 provides much clearer PRS-only performance reporting.

PGS001777 is more directly disease-focused and endpoint-faithful to the target: trait_reported is explicitly alcohol-related cirrhosis and the publication is centered on predicting development of alcohol-related cirrhosis in drinkers, whereas PGS000704 comes from a broad biomarker genetics paper (framework-like context) even though its trait_reported matches. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model C-index/AUROC (0.711 for PGS000704 vs 0.671 for PGS001777) is not a clean PRS comparator; additionally PGS001777 provides a strong risk-gradient metric (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 6.18) supportive of meaningful stratification, while PGS000704’s per-SD HR=1.18 suggests weaker PRS signal. Despite PGS000704’s much larger training/validation and genome-wide variant count, the combination of disease-focused endpoint context and stronger effect-size evidence makes PGS001777 better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper with identical covariates (age/sex/array/PCs) and the same DEV/EVAL ancestry distribution, so the decision rests on endpoint fidelity and PRS-only metrics. PGS001262 uses a direct doctor-diagnosed angina phenotype (“Vascular/heart problems diagnosed by doctor Angina”), which is a straightforward disease-status endpoint for angina pectoris, whereas PGS001261 is explicitly time-to-event (“TTE angina pectoris”), a weaker match for a generic angina pectoris target absent other advantages. Performance is very similar, but PGS001262 is slightly higher on PRS-only AUROC (0.5868 vs 0.5823) and PRS-only R² (0.01304 vs 0.01228), both plausible under the heritability ceiling; PGS001261’s larger training N and variant count are weak tie-breakers here. Overall edge to PGS001262, but confidence is low because differences are small.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo aortic stenosis; incident case phenotyping) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on effect-size evidence and design comparability. PGS005254 shows a clearly reported HR per SD with CI (HR=1.64, 1.50–1.78) under a basic covariate set (age, age^2, sex, PCs), which is more directly interpretable as PRS signal than PGS005252’s full-model C-index=0.87 that is likely covariate-driven given its much heavier clinical covariates (multiple comorbidities and BMI/smoking/renal failure) and no incremental/PRS-only metric. While PGS005252 has a larger validation sample and a higher HR point estimate (1.92), that HR is presented without CI and alongside covariate-heavy modeling, reducing comparability. Overall, PGS005254 provides cleaner, more PRS-attributable evidence for aortic stenosis risk.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is directly aligned (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Alcohol use disorder; trait_efo = alcohol dependence) and it provides stronger PRS-discrimination evidence via an OR top 10% vs rest of 1.76 (plus β=0.17), whereas PGS000201 targets a more measurement/proxy-like construct (trait_reported = Problematic alcohol use; trait_efo = alcohol dependence measurement) and only reports a small incremental ΔR²=0.01192 (with β=0.099). Neither candidate reports clean PRS-only AUC/R², so effect-size strength and endpoint fidelity dominate; additionally, PGS002739’s multi-cohort development context (MVP/PGC/UKB) and AFR evaluation focus support robustness for AUD in its evaluated population, while PGS000201 is UKB-trained and EUR-only evaluated with heavier stated covariate adjustment, making its reported incremental metric less directly comparable.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): it has exact trait alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo both aortic stenosis) and endpoint fidelity (incident aortic stenosis cases). While neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, PGS005252 shows a stronger effect size signal (HR=1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255), suggesting materially better PRS discrimination. PGS005255 is less endpoint-faithful on its surface label (trait_reported is mean pressure gradient; trait_efo includes aortic measurement) even though phenotyping_reported mentions incident aortic stenosis, making it more mixed as a direct aortic stenosis PRS. PGS005252’s full-model C-index=0.87 is not PRS-comparable and is covariate-heavy, but it still provides some supportive evidence; overall the stronger HR and cleaner trait labeling outweigh PGS005255’s larger training N and simpler covariates.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and neither provides a PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS003972 is better supported by study archetype and construction context: it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis (many contributing cohorts listed) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with larger variant coverage (1,118,997 vs 592,187). PGS002054 is from a UKB portability/framework paper (single-cohort development) with only a small partial-r (0.0144) as the visible performance signal and no clearer PRS-comparable discrimination; its multi-ancestry evaluation breadth is a plus but doesn’t outweigh the framework penalty and weaker disease-focused evidence. PGS003972’s reported AUROC=0.69 is full-model and not PRS-comparable, so it’s not decisive, but overall the disease-focused multi-cohort context and broader genome-wide model support make it the stronger pick.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics don’t differentiate directly. PGS000753 is from a disease-focused AAA genetic-architecture study (MVP/Mayo-VDB) with a clear AAA endpoint (prevalent AAA) and provides a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.37), which is directly interpretable as PRS signal. PGS002054 comes from a UK Biobank portability/framework paper (“Portability of 245 polygenic scores…”) and only reports a very small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0144) without effect-size context; despite its larger genome-wide model and broader evaluation ancestries, the framework archetype and weaker visible PRS signal make it less well-supported for selecting a primary AAA PRS here.

PGS002738 is the better match to the target trait (alcohol dependence) on endpoint fidelity: it is explicitly an Alcohol Use Disorder case/control-style endpoint (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both “Alcohol use disorder”, trait_efo “alcohol dependence”). PGS000201 is closer to an alcohol-use/measurement construct (“Problematic alcohol use”, trait_efo “alcohol dependence measurement”) and its phenotyping is a DSM-5 criteria count (log-transformed), which is less directly aligned to dependence as a diagnosis. Neither candidate reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics don’t separate them; however PGS002738 provides a stronger discriminative signal via OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96, whereas PGS000201 only shows a small ΔR²=0.01192. Training context also favors PGS002738 (MVP+UKB vs UKB-only), with similar EUR-only evaluation sizes, making PGS002738 overall better-supported despite unknown covariates.

PGS004913 is explicitly disease-focused and endpoint-faithful to the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis”), whereas PGS000704 comes from a broad UKB biomarker genetics framework paper, making it more likely a pan-trait/byproduct score despite the similar label (“Alcoholic cirrhosis”). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so PGS000704’s full-model C-index=0.711 cannot be treated as PRS discrimination evidence; in contrast PGS004913 provides more directly PRS-informative effect-size evidence (OR top vs bottom deciles=4.4) alongside basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and a study designed around cirrhosis risk among heavy drinkers. Both are largely EUR-evaluated, but PGS004913’s tighter phenotype/study alignment outweighs PGS000704’s larger UKB training/validation and genome-wide variant count given the framework-context and non-comparable metric reporting.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (M13 Other arthritis), same EFO mapping (arthritis), same publication, same UKB training cohort and training N (174,489), same EUR-only development/evaluation, same variant count (1,059,939), and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (no pgs_only_auc/r2). With metrics absent, the main differentiator is the available PRS effect size: PGS004547 reports a higher OR per SD (1.262) than PGS004477 (1.196), indicating stronger PRS signal in the same validation context. Method differences (RFDiseasemetaPRS vs LDpred2) are secondary here, but are compatible with the stronger effect size for PGS004547.

PGS002755 is the stronger-supported atopic eczema PRS because it targets the generic disease endpoint (trait_reported: atopic dermatitis; phenotyping_reported: incident atopic dermatitis) with a modern genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) and very large European evaluation (n=337,910), and it provides a PRS-linked effect size (HR high vs low PRS=1.249). In contrast, PGS001773 is restricted to a narrower subtype endpoint (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis) and its only strong-looking metrics are full-model AUROC/R² (0.93/0.49) with covariates including parental ethnicity, which are not PRS-comparable and are implausibly high relative to eczema heritability, suggesting covariate-driven inflation rather than standalone PRS performance. Both lack PRS-only AUC/R², so the decision rests on endpoint generality + method/scale, favoring PGS002755.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported=incident atopic dermatitis) and have similarly light covariates and identical EUR evaluation size (n=337,910), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. PGS002755 is better-supported structurally: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and comes from a broad cross-disease PRS benchmarking paper, whereas PGS004587 is a very sparse 23-SNP genome-wide-significant score from an exposure-focused air-pollution study (more risk of being an auxiliary genetic-risk term rather than an optimized eczema PRS). The available effect-size evidence is also slightly stronger for PGS002755 (HR high vs low 1.249 vs 1.153).

PGS004587 is the better-supported match to the target trait (atopic eczema) because its endpoint is a general atopic dermatitis diagnosis framed as incident disease (phenotyping_reported: "Incident atopic dermatitis"), aligning well with the generic atopic eczema concept, and it is evaluated in a very large European cohort (EVAL EUR, n=337,910). Although it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R², it at least reports a PRS-stratified effect size (HR high vs low PRS 1.153). In contrast, PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype ("Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis"), has much smaller validation (n=676), and its impressive AUROC/R² (0.93/0.49) are full-model/non-PRS-only metrics and are likely inflated by covariates including parental ethnicity (family/ancestry packaging), making the performance evidence less comparable and less trustworthy for standalone PRS quality.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to atrial fibrillation (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model discrimination values are not directly comparable PRS metrics. PGS005168’s very high C-index (0.8718) is heavily discounted because its covariates include the named clinical risk calculator CHARGE-AF (risk-wrapper packaging), making the reported performance likely covariate-driven rather than PRS-driven. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), avoiding that packaging concern, and it provides strong PRS effect-size evidence (OR 1.82 with tight CI) plus a method/structure advantage (PRS-CSx with substantially more variants, 1.27M vs 0.38M) and broader stated validation ancestry coverage. Overall, PGS005313 is better-supported as a standalone AF PRS on the visible fields.

PGS001263 is the better-supported match for the target trait (atrial flutter) because its endpoint is directly aligned: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all specifically “Atrial flutter,” whereas PGS001339 explicitly bundles atrial fibrillation with flutter and uses a time-to-event phenotype (“TTE atrial fibrillation and flutter”), which is a weaker fidelity match for a generic atrial flutter target. Performance evidence is essentially tied and slightly favors PGS001263 on PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.617 vs 0.613; PGS-only R² 0.02517 vs 0.02447), with identical training cohort (UKB), training N, covariates, and validation N; ancestry evaluation breadth is similar and not decisive. Given near-clone framework context, the cleaner phenotype specificity plus marginally better PRS-only metrics makes PGS001263 the stronger choice.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUCs are not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. However, PGS005168’s reported performance is explicitly packaged with the CHARGE-AF clinical risk calculator in the covariates, a strong negative signal for PRS comparability (its high C-index 0.8718 is likely largely covariate-driven). PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that risk-wrapper leakage, and still shows strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.94). While PGS005168 has a more polygenic method/variant count (PRS-CS; 382,963 variants) and larger EUR validation (52,757 vs 24,147), the CHARGE-AF packaging makes its reported discrimination less informative for PRS quality than the cleaner design of PGS002814.

PGS001263 is the better-supported choice for the target trait atrial flutter because it has exact endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”) and reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R²=0.025), which are interpretable and pass the heritability-ceiling sanity check (R² well below the provided h2_obs). In contrast, PGS002050 uses a broader combined endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”) rather than flutter-specific, and it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only partial correlation is provided), making its predictive evidence less directly comparable for flutter specifically despite larger training size, many more variants, and a portability-focused study context.

PGS001339 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance for the target endpoint: it reports explicit PRS-only AUROC=0.613 and PRS-only R2=0.02447 (no covariates), which is interpretable and passes the heritability ceiling sanity check (h2_obs≈0.0157; scale differences aside, it is not an implausible outlier). It also provides incremental AUROC and clearly states a time-to-event phenotype for AF/flutter. In contrast, PGS002050 has aligned trait fields but provides no PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only partial correlation=0.1034), making its predictive strength less directly comparable/transparent despite a larger variant count and training N. Both are UKB framework-style scores with similar basic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation, so the decisive visible advantage is PGS001339’s cleaner PRS-only metric evidence.

Both candidates match the target trait (asthma) with acceptable endpoint fidelity, but PGS001782 is better supported structurally and by study archetype: it comes from a global multi-biobank PRS development context (many training/development cohorts) using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with very large variant coverage (884,043), which is generally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than the very sparse UKB pan-trait framework score PGS001344 (snpnet; 6,139 variants; publication explicitly “across 813 traits”). Although PGS001344 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.646/0.0597) and a larger validation n, it is penalized by the portability/pan-trait framework archetype that tends to generalize worse; meanwhile PGS001782 provides a PRS-comparable covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 (0.0488) with basic covariates and remains below the asthma heritability ceiling, supporting plausibility. Overall, the multi-cohort genome-wide score (PGS001782) is the more reliable choice despite slightly lower reported PRS-only R2 and missing PRS-only AUROC.

PGS000327 is the better-supported ASD PRS because its endpoint fidelity is coherent and direct: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to “Autism spectrum disorder,” and it comes from an ASD-focused Nat Genet GWAS meta-analysis with explicit training cohorts and sample size plus an interpretable effect size (OR=1.33). In contrast, PGS002790 has an explicit phenotype mismatch (phenotyping_reported = “Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)”) despite the ASD label, suggesting weaker endpoint specificity/possible metadata contamination; it also lacks training sample size and reports only a small partial R² (0.0055) with no effect sizes. Both lack PRS-only AUC/R², so the decisive factors are phenotype alignment and study archetype, which clearly favor PGS000327.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a clean differentiator. PGS005313 is better supported structurally and for transportability: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage cross-ancestry method (PRS-CSx) with far more variants (1,271,239 vs 4,520) and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (European, African unspecified, South Asian, East Asian, Hispanic/LatAm, Other) rather than East-Asian-only evaluation for PGS002814. Performance evidence is also at least as strong via effect size (OR 1.82 for PGS005313 vs OR 1.94 for PGS002814; similar magnitude), while the small full-model AUROC difference (0.78 vs 0.74) is secondary given both are covariate-adjusted. Overall, PGS005313 has the clearer multi-ancestry, genome-wide PRS evidence package; confidence is moderate because both rely on full-model metrics and PGS002814 has explicit large training N and a reported pseudo-R2 that is not directly PRS-only.

PGS002727 is more endpoint-faithful to the target asthma use-case because its phenotyping is explicitly "Pediatric asthma" and it comes from a disease-focused pediatric asthma paper, whereas PGS001782 is from a global biobank portability/framework study ("Global Biobank analyses...") which domain guidance flags as typically underperforming disease-focused models unless it has clearly superior endpoint+metric evidence. While PGS001782 does report a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.048844) with basic covariates, its evidence package is otherwise thin (single performance record, no effect sizes, EUR-only evaluation). PGS002727 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC=0.66/R2=0.04), but it provides strong PRS signal via OR=1.57 per SD and much broader multi-ancestry evaluation context plus very large validation (n=391,820), making it better-supported overall despite the metric comparability limitation.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates, training cohort (UKB), training N, and identical reported partial-r (~0.0716) with the same multi-ancestry evaluation mix, so performance/phenotype context does not differentiate them. With metrics essentially tied and no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002032 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (19,768 variants) versus PGS001824’s very sparse penalized regression model (22 variants). Given the same study family and identical observed partial-r, the broader genome-wide model is better-supported as capturing polygenic signal for this trait.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sample sizes, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not decisive). With endpoints and design effectively identical, the only differentiators are small, likely-noise differences in full-model AUROC and pseudo-R², where PGS000452 is slightly higher (AUROC 0.632 vs 0.630; Nagelkerke R² 0.0487 vs 0.0456). PGS000456 has a slightly higher top-1% OR, but overall evidence is too close, so PGS000452 wins on marginally better overall discrimination metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training N (11,734), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same validation N (11,322), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R2, which are not decisive PRS-comparable metrics). With endpoints and study context effectively identical, the only differentiators are small, likely-noise performance differences and method/structure: PGS000454 (P+T, 27 variants) has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.632 vs 0.630) and higher pseudo-R² (0.0489 vs 0.0456), while PGS000456 (GWAS hits, 30 variants) has slightly higher top-1% OR (3.95 vs 3.79). Given the lack of PRS-only metrics and minimal gaps, I pick PGS000454 on the marginally stronger overall discrimination summary (AUROC and pseudo-R²) under identical covariates.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002787 is specifically bipolar I disorder (a subtype mismatch for a broad target). Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), have similar variant counts and EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only small partial R² full-model values), so performance evidence does not clearly differentiate them; the slightly higher partial R² in PGS002787 is not decisive given endpoint fidelity. Validation N differences are minor. Hence PGS002786 wins on phenotype alignment, but confidence is low due to weak/indirect performance metrics and both having non-disease phenotyping_reported fields.

PGS001824 is the better-supported match to the target trait (bilirubin metabolism disease) on endpoint fidelity: its trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are directly “Disorders of bilirubin excretion” mapped solely to bilirubin metabolism disease, whereas PGS000924 uses a broader combined endpoint (“disorders of porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism”) and is explicitly time-to-event, both of which dilute alignment to the target. Although PGS000924 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2, those metrics are internally inconsistent with the provided heritability ceiling for bilirubin (~0.089) because its PGS-only R2=0.218 exceeds that ceiling, making the performance evidence suspect/non-comparable for this target. Both are UKB-derived framework-style scores with basic covariates and similar ancestry evaluation patterns, so the decision hinges on phenotype specificity and metric sanity, favoring PGS001824.

PGS002032 is the better-supported choice for the target "bilirubin metabolism disease" because its endpoint is a direct match (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both "Disorders of bilirubin excretion" mapped to the target EFO) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with a large variant set (19,768) and explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), which is supportive for transportability. PGS000924 comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework ("across 813 traits"; snpnet) with an extremely sparse 5-variant model and a time-to-event composite phenotype that also includes porphyrin metabolism disease (less endpoint-fidelitous to bilirubin metabolism disease alone). Although PGS000924 reports clean PGS-only AUROC/R2, the reported PGS-only R2=0.218 exceeds the provided local heritability ceiling (~0.089), making the metric suspect/non-comparable for this trait and reducing its evidentiary value versus the more coherent endpoint/method package of PGS002032.

PGS002727 is the better-supported asthma PRS for the target use because it is disease-focused and endpoint-specific ("Multiancestral polygenic risk score for pediatric asthma"; phenotyping_reported="Pediatric asthma") with strong PRS signal evidence via OR=1.57 per SD and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS; ~986k variants) plus very broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS) and very large overall validation (n=391,820). PGS001344 does report clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.6457; PGS R2=0.0597, below the asthma h2_liability ceiling) and uses only basic covariates, but it comes from a pan-trait UKB sparse-framework paper ("across 813 traits"; snpnet; 6,139 variants; UKB-only development), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external generalization than a disease-focused multi-ancestry score. The main drawback for PGS002727 is that its AUROC/R2 shown are full-model (not PRS-only) and covariates are unknown, so confidence is not high, but overall the study archetype + endpoint focus + multi-ancestry evaluation favor PGS002727 over the framework-derived PGS001344.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait/phenotyping alignment to basal cell carcinoma, same publication/family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same full-model AUROC (0.632) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (so full-model AUROC can’t differentiate PRS quality). The only visible empirical edge is slightly stronger performance in PGS000454: marginally higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0489 vs 0.0487) and higher top-1% vs rest OR (3.79 vs 3.61), with essentially identical per-SD OR. Given the tiny differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is low, but PGS000454 is better-supported on the available discrimination/effect-size fields.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002788 targets the narrower subtype bipolar II disorder. Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), have similar EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical covariates (age, PCs1-3), same validation sample size (n=2,524), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only small full-model partial R² values). Although PGS002788 has a slightly higher reported partial R² (0.00307 vs 0.00251), the endpoint fidelity advantage of PGS002786 to the requested broad bipolar disorder outweighs this small, non-PRS-only metric difference.

PGS001033 is the better-supported choice for the broad target "blood coagulation disease" because it maps directly to that EFO term and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.634 and PGS-only R²=0.0578) with only basic covariates, plus broader multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS). PGS002034 targets a narrower congenital clotting-factor deficiency (different EFO than the target) and, while it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many variants, it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² and reports only partial-r, making its predictive evidence less directly comparable for this head-to-head.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size, ancestry distribution, and validation size; and their only reported performance signal (partial-r) is essentially identical (0.0563 vs 0.0562). With metrics unable to differentiate, the structural tie-break favors PGS002034 because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (32,552 vs 45), which is generally more capable of capturing polygenic signal than an extremely sparse penalized-regression score when all else is equal.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication, same SDPR method, similar genome-wide variant counts (~935k), EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, same basic covariates (age, PCs1-3), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only small full-model partial R² values). Endpoint fidelity to the target trait “bipolar disorder” is slightly better for PGS002787 because it targets bipolar I disorder (Type 1), which is closer to the generic bipolar disorder umbrella than the bipolar II–specific PGS002788; the differing phenotyping_reported fields look behavior/proxy-like for both and don’t clearly favor either. PGS002788 has a trivially higher partial R² and slightly larger validation N, but these are weak tie-breakers and the metric difference is negligible, so the subtype alignment drives a low-confidence win for PGS002787.

PGS001033 is the better-supported choice for the broad target "blood coagulation disease" because it maps directly to that EFO term and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.634 and PGS-only R²=0.0578 with only basic covariates), plus broader multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS). In contrast, PGS001826 targets a narrower congenital clotting-factor deficiency EFO (not the generic blood coagulation disease umbrella) and lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R², reporting only partial correlation; despite larger training N and more variants, its endpoint specificity mismatch and weaker comparable metric evidence make it less supported for the stated target.

Both candidates match the target trait (trait_efo=breast carcinoma), but PGS000015 has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a PRS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.027 (and this is below the provided liability h2 ceiling 0.1715, so it passes the sanity check). PGS000332 reports only a full-model C-index=0.75 with no PRS-only AUC/R2, and its covariates include family history plus multiple lifestyle/reproductive/HRT variables, making the reported discrimination more clinically packaged and less informative about standalone PRS quality. Although PGS000332 uses LDpred with far more variants, the lack of PRS-only metrics and heavier covariate set make it less directly supported than PGS000015 for a generic breast carcinoma PRS.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to celiac disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported AUROCs are full-model and not cleanly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Given that limitation, PGS000040 has the stronger structural/evidence package: it is a disease-focused genomic prediction model with a substantially larger variant set (228 vs 53) and a slightly higher reported full-model AUROC (0.90 vs 0.879), with consistent EUR development/evaluation. PGS000316’s main differentiator is much larger validation sample size and training n, but validation size is a weak tie-break and its AUROC is also full-model with unknown covariates, offering no clearer PRS-only signal than PGS000040.

PGS000040 is a disease-focused celiac/coeliac disease model with exact endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Coeliac disease”), whereas PGS001301 comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework (“across 813 traits”) and uses a broader/less specific endpoint label (“Malabsorption/coeliac disease”), which is a mild phenotype-alignment penalty. Although PGS001301 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.8287; PGS-only R2 0.1422) and basic covariates, its framework archetype is a known generalization risk; by contrast, PGS000040’s reported AUROC=0.9 is full-model only (not PRS-comparable) but the overall record is more directly targeted to celiac disease. Given endpoint fidelity is the top-ranked criterion and the framework penalty is substantial, PGS000040 is better-supported overall despite weaker PRS-only metric reporting.

PGS003428 is better supported as a standalone cervical carcinoma PRS: it is disease-focused (cervical phenotypes meta-analysis) with an explicit incident cervical cancer endpoint and a genome-wide LDpred construction (2.89M variants), and it shows a stronger PRS effect size (HR 1.33) than PGS005165 (HR 1.2). Both candidates only report full-model C-index (no PRS-only AUC/R2), so the small C-index difference (0.613 vs 0.566) is secondary; however PGS003428’s covariates (age, smoking) are still light and its larger validation (128k vs 57k) mildly supports robustness. PGS005165 comes from a pan-cancer risk framework in a single EAS cohort and uses only 15 known loci, which is structurally weaker for a polygenic disease endpoint absent clearly superior PRS-only metrics.

PGS000015 is better supported for the target breast carcinoma because it has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a PRS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.027 (and overall R2 matches), which is interpretable as PRS contribution and is below the provided liability h2 ceiling (~0.17). PGS000007 reports only a full-model AUROC=0.78 with no PRS-only AUC/R2, so its apparent performance advantage is not comparable as a standalone PRS metric. Endpoint fidelity also favors PGS000015: phenotyping_reported is simply “Breast cancer,” whereas PGS000007 uses “Breast Cancer (personal history),” a weaker survivor/history phenotype for generic disease-risk prediction. Both are EUR-trained and have multi-ancestry evaluation, but PGS000015 also has much larger validation (n=157,895 vs n=9,529), providing broader support once endpoint/metric comparability is satisfied.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size (n=19,908), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial-r). With performance essentially tied (partial-r 0.098 for PGS002072 vs 0.0948 for PGS001861, overlapping CIs), the main differentiator is structural: PGS002072 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (428,587 vs 2,059), which is generally favored for polygenic disease architectures when other evidence is indistinguishable. Therefore PGS002072 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident cervical cancer; EUR evaluation). However, PGS003428 is from a cervical-phenotype GWAS meta-analysis explicitly aimed at cervical phenotypes/risk stratification and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred; ~2.9M variants) with multi-cohort development (EB, FinnGen, KP, UKB), which is structurally and archetypically stronger support for a standalone PRS than PGS000073’s very sparse 10-variant GWAS-hits score from a cross-cancer evaluation framework. The higher reported full-model AUROC/C-index for PGS000073 (0.745/0.75 vs 0.613) is not PRS-only and is further confounded by a much heavier covariate set (parity, oral contraceptive use, pack-years, PCs, array), so it is discounted as evidence of PRS quality; meanwhile PGS003428 has cleaner covariates (age, smoking) and a slightly stronger per-SD HR (1.33 vs 1.22).

PGS001174 is the better-supported match to the target trait cholelithiasis because its endpoint is directly aligned (trait_efo=cholelithiasis; phenotyping_reported=TTE cholelithiasis) and it reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.623 and PGS-only R2=0.028), which are interpretable and plausibly below the trait heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS001861 uses a broader composite endpoint (cholelithiasis and cholecystitis; trait_efo includes both) and provides only a partial-correlation metric without PRS-only AUROC/R2, making cross-model PRS performance comparison weaker despite its larger training N and more variants. Both are UKB framework-style scores with basic covariates, so the decisive advantage is PGS001174’s tighter phenotype fidelity and clearer PRS-only metric evidence.

PGS001174 is a direct match to the target (trait_efo=cholelithiasis; phenotyping_reported=TTE cholelithiasis) and, crucially, reports clean PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.623 and PGS-only R²=0.028) with basic covariates; its PRS-only R² is also plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.021). In contrast, PGS002072 has a broader/combined endpoint (cholelithiasis and cholecystitis; trait_efo includes cholecystitis) and provides no PRS-comparable AUROC/R²—only a partial correlation—making its predictive evidence less directly comparable for cholelithiasis despite larger variant count and training N. Both are UKB framework-style scores with multi-ancestry evaluation, so the decisive advantage is PGS001174’s tighter endpoint and PRS-only metrics.

PGS000316 has cleaner endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both explicitly “Coeliac disease”), and it comes from a disease-focused clinical-care pilot study, whereas PGS001301 is a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a broader/less specific phenotype label (“Malabsorption/coeliac disease”), which is a known weaker archetype for external reliability. Although PGS001301 reports explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.8287; PGS-only R² 0.1422) and basic covariates, those metrics come from the sparse UKB framework context and the R² is high enough relative to the provided celiac h2_liability (~0.23) to warrant some caution about scale/comparability; meanwhile PGS000316 lacks PRS-only metrics (only full-model AUROC 0.879, not directly comparable) but avoids the framework penalty and matches the disease endpoint more directly. Overall, endpoint/study archetype outweigh the metric-format advantage here, but the absence of PRS-only metrics for PGS000316 keeps confidence low.

PGS002237 is better supported for chronic kidney disease because its endpoint is more specific and clinically anchored (stage 3+ with explicit eGFR <45 definition) and it comes from a CKD-focused across-ancestries study with broader evaluation ancestries (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE) and a larger development sample (n=279,819). Although both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R² and only report full-model AUROC, PGS002237 also shows a slightly stronger effect size (OR 1.47 vs 1.39 for PGS004158). PGS004158 has a much larger validation N and an ensemble-style method name, but its phenotyping is broader/less specific (“CKD or dialysis”) and its reported AUROC is low and not PRS-comparable; overall the phenotype fidelity and cross-ancestry support favor PGS002237.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; trait_reported cervical cancer) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index/AUROC is only weakly informative. PGS000073 has stronger reported discrimination/effect evidence in its selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.745; C-index 0.75; HR 1.22) versus PGS005165 (C-index 0.566; HR 1.2), and it is supported by a larger evaluation sample (211,795 vs 57,359). While PGS000073 uses more epidemiologic covariates (parity, oral contraceptive use, smoking pack-years) that could inflate full-model metrics compared with PGS005165’s mostly demographic/PC covariates, the performance gap is large enough that PGS000073 remains better-supported overall on the visible fields.

PGS000332 has stronger endpoint fidelity for the target breast carcinoma via an explicit incident breast cancer phenotype, whereas PGS000007 is based on “Breast Cancer (personal history),” which is a weaker survivor/history-enriched endpoint for generic disease-risk prediction. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model discrimination), so the small full-model metric difference (0.78 for PGS000007 vs 0.75 C-index for PGS000332) is not a reliable PRS comparator—especially since PGS000332’s model includes family history and other clinical covariates that can inflate full-model performance. With PRS-only metrics absent for both, structural signals favor PGS000332’s genome-wide LDpred score with far broader variant coverage (6.39M vs 3,820), which is generally advantageous for a polygenic cancer trait. PGS000007 does have broader evaluation ancestry, but its weaker phenotype definition and sparse model leave PGS000332 better supported overall.

Both candidates match the target trait (CKD stage ≥3) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the very high full-model AUROC values (0.78 in PGS002237; 0.90 in PGS005090) are not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS002237 is better supported overall because it has clearer endpoint fidelity via an explicit phenotyping definition (eGFR <45 ml/min/1.73m²) and, crucially, broader external evaluation across multiple ancestries (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE) rather than the AFR-only GWAS/EVAL context of PGS005090. While PGS005090 has a larger validation sample and a method/variant-count advantage (PRS-CS; 1.14M variants), its training sample size is not reported and its performance evidence is limited to a single record with full-model metrics only, making it less well-supported on the visible fields than the multi-ancestry, explicitly phenotyped Nat Med score PGS002237.

PGS005090 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint is more specific and clinically aligned (CKD stage 3 or higher; phenotyping_reported: chronic kidney disease) and it comes from a CKD-in-Black-American-populations focused study with AFR-only GWAS and AFR-only evaluation, matching its stated evaluation ancestry. Although its reported AUROC=0.9 is only a full-model metric and likely covariate-influenced (age/sex/diabetes/PCs), it also provides an effect size (OR 1.41) and a large external validation sample (n=67,819) in the intended ancestry context. In contrast, PGS004158 is from a general multi-biobank methods evaluation framework, has a broader/less clean phenotype definition ("chronic kidney disease or dialysis"), and its only visible performance is also full-model (AUROC ~0.59, R² ~0.02) with covariates listed as 0, making cross-record comparability limited; it also mixes evaluation ancestries (EUR/SAS) while being developed in EUR only. With neither candidate providing PRS-only AUC/R², the stronger endpoint fidelity and disease/ancestry-focused study context favor PGS005090.

PGS001783 is better supported for COPD because it shows substantially stronger PRS-comparable performance (Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2 = 0.0381) than PGS001332’s very weak PRS-only metrics (PGS-only R2 = 0.00235; PGS-only AUROC = 0.5397). PGS001783’s PRS-only R2 also aligns with the provided COPD heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0388), suggesting a plausible, non-inflated PRS signal, whereas PGS001332’s high full-model AUROC (~0.73) is explicitly undermined by tiny incremental AUROC (0.003), indicating covariate-driven discrimination rather than PRS strength. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both, but PGS001332 comes from a known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“813 traits” snpnet) with a very small variant set (482), a pattern associated with poorer external generalization; PGS001783 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRS-CS-auto) with ~884k variants and multi-biobank GWAS context, which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease like COPD despite its smaller EUR-only evaluation sample.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Corneal dystrophy”), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation size (same). PGS004621 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are directly “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver,” whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to “Alcoholic cirrhosis” (a subtype/etiology-specific endpoint mismatch for a generic cirrhosis target). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC/C-index values (0.68 vs 0.711) are not cleanly comparable; in that setting, PGS004621 has stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR 1.42 vs HR 1.18, suggesting more discriminative genetic contribution) and a more externally oriented, disease-focused multi-cohort development/validation context (multiple biobanks; very large EUR evaluation n=1,153,995) compared with PGS000704’s single-UKB framework-style origin. Overall, endpoint fidelity plus stronger effect-size evidence favors PGS004621.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Cirrhosis”). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we should not treat PGS004621’s full-model AUROC=0.68 as a standalone PRS metric. However, PGS004621 has stronger structural and study-support signals: a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and very large European evaluation (n=1,153,995) across many biobanks, with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). PGS000726 is a much sparser 12-variant GWS score with smaller validation (n=30,469) and no discrimination metrics; while it reports a stronger tail-contrast OR (top vs bottom quintile OR=2.26), overall it has weaker polygenic coverage and less robust evaluation context. Given cirrhosis is not clearly a single-locus trait, the genome-wide PRS-CS model is better-supported on the visible metadata.

ontology: congenital vitamin k-dependent coagulation factors deficiency

PGS004536 is better supported for COPD despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R2 because it is a disease-focused COPD ICD10 endpoint (J44) and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=1.49 per SD), which is near the “strong” threshold and provides meaningful PRS-specific evidence. While PGS001332 has explicit PRS-only metrics and broader evaluation ancestries, the framework/sparse-model penalty plus weak PRS-only signal makes it less compelling than the stronger disease-anchored OR evidence in PGS004536.

Both candidates are near-clones for CAD (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, same method LDpred2, same training n=116,649, same basic covariates, same validation sample size), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural and effect-size evidence. Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/all-cause dementia; trait_efo=dementia), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS004281 (0.819 vs 0.761) is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage. PGS003333 is the better-supported depressive-disorder PRS on visible fields: it has tighter endpoint fidelity (explicit Major Depressive Disorder in both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported, matching the target depressive disorder) and clearer disease-focused development context (training_development_cohorts listed: 23andMe/PGC/UKB) than PGS002759, which is more generic (“Depression”) and provides no training cohort provenance. PGS003576 is better supported for depressive disorder because its endpoint is explicitly major depressive disorder (lifetime) with phenotyping_reported as major depressive disorder, and it provides substantially richer study/transportability context: defined training cohort (UKB), training n=67,164, and multi-ancestry evaluation (including EUR plus AFR/AMR/ASN/EAS) with a larger validation sample (n=42,250). PGS000997 is better supported on comparable PRS evidence for diverticular disease: it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.591 and PGS-only R²=0.0178) with basic covariates and provides multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), whereas PGS004544 provides no AUROC/R² at all (only an OR=1.32) and has unknown covariates, making its predictive performance and comparability harder to judge. PGS004254 is the better-supported Crohn’s disease PRS on endpoint fidelity and study archetype: it targets a direct Crohn’s disease diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both Crohn’s disease) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto; 744,682 variants), which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than the very sparse snpnet score in PGS001330 (220 variants) from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” framework. Although PGS001330 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.5759; PGS-only R2 0.00621, below the h2_obs ceiling ~0.0122) and has multi-ancestry evaluation, its endpoint is explicitly time-to-event (TTE), and the framework/sparse construction is a strong negative generalization signal versus a disease-focused score. PGS004254 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC 0.72) so the metric evidence is less directly comparable, but it does provide a strong per-SD effect size (OR 2.18) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), supporting meaningful PRS signal; overall this outweighs the modest PRS-only performance and framework penalty of PGS001330.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to dupuytren contracture (same EFO; phenotyping_reported matches). PGS001254 has clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.6646; PGS R2 0.0247) but comes from the pan-trait UKB sparse-PRS framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 11-variant model and EUR-only evaluation, which is a known generalization risk. PGS001880, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, is a genome-wide penalized regression score with far more variants (2443) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger transportability evidence and a PRS-comparable partial-r signal. Given the framework/sparsity penalty on PGS001254 and the broader evaluation/structure of PGS001880, PGS001880 is better-supported overall despite missing AUROC/R2.

PGS002304 is the cleaner endpoint match to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” whereas PGS000644 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” despite mapping to the same EFO, creating endpoint-fidelity ambiguity. Given stronger phenotype alignment plus slightly better reported discrimination, PGS002304 is better supported overall.

PGS004614 is the better-supported choice for generic diverticular disease risk because it is disease-focused with a direct diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Diverticular disease”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (SBayesR) with very broad variant coverage (1,082,282), plus multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/SAS). Net: PGS004614 wins on endpoint fidelity + disease-focused context + method/coverage, while PGS000997’s main advantage is modest PRS-only metrics from a framework score.

PGS004614 is the better-supported diverticular disease PRS because it comes from a disease-focused diverticular-disease genetics paper and shows explicit validation discrimination (AUROC 0.76) in the record, whereas PGS004544 provides no AUC/R2 at all (only an OR=1.32, which is moderate). Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity to diverticular disease (PGS004614: generic diverticular disease; PGS004544: ICD10 K57 diverticular disease of intestine), but PGS004614’s reported covariates include family history (making its full-model AUROC less PRS-comparable), while PGS004544’s covariates are unknown and its publication framing (“integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”) suggests risk-factor packaging rather than a clean standalone disease PRS. Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to dupuytren contracture (same EFO; phenotyping_reported matches the disease). PGS002304 is the better-supported match for the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is exact: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both “Follicular lymphoma” (trait_efo also matches). Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size (n=18,971), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), come from the same publication, have the same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.639 for PGS005270 vs 0.630 for PGS005271) is not a reliable differentiator. Both candidates are near-clones for the target hyperthyroidism via the clinically dominant subtype Graves’ disease (same trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported, same method PRSCS, same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size n=94,651, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator). PGS001320 has clean, PRS-comparable performance reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R2=0.06493 with explicit “no covariates” metrics) on an endpoint that matches the target trait (“Hypertension”), with basic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation listed. Given the domain guidance not to substitute full-model AUROC for PRS-only metrics, PGS001320 is better-supported on the visible fields despite the framework-paper penalty.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_efo hypertension; phenotyping_reported prevalent hypertension), come from the same Nat Commun paper, have the same training N (10,314), evaluation N (39,035), evaluation ancestry (MAE 100%), and similarly covariate-inflated full-model AUROC (~0.764 vs 0.763) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported—so performance metrics don’t differentiate. PGS004236 is better supported because it provides additional PRS-relevant evidence (reports an OR=2.1 per SD with CI) that PGS004234 lacks, and it appears to be the more comprehensive multi-cohort development (BioMe+MVP+UKB vs BioMe+UKB) with a larger variant set (398,805 vs 234,228), which is a favorable structural signal when endpoints/covariates are otherwise identical.

PGS001320 is the better-supported standalone PRS for hypertension because it reports clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R²=0.06493 with basic covariates listed separately), enabling direct assessment of genetic signal and a heritability-ceiling sanity check. In contrast, PGS004236 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.764) with a substantially heavier covariate set (including BMI and smoking), and provides no PGS-only AUROC/R², so its discrimination is not comparable and may be largely covariate-driven despite a strong OR (2.1). Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both, but PGS004236’s phenotyping is explicitly prevalent hypertension, while PGS001320 uses a generic hypertension phenotype; overall the metric cleanliness and comparability favor PGS001320, though confidence is moderated because PGS001320 comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper while PGS004236 is disease-focused and multi-ethnic.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to the umbrella JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly for the oligoarticular JIA subtype (endpoint mismatch for a generic JIA target). Both are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), same EUR-only dev/eval ancestry, and similarly basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS000325 (0.80 vs 0.738) is not decisive. Given comparable design but stronger endpoint fidelity, PGS000114 wins despite PGS000325’s larger validation N and higher full-model AUROC.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Disorders of iron metabolism”), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (same distribution; n=19,883). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiators are structural and the available PRS-comparable metric: PGS002031 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with many more variants (6,713 vs 654) and shows slightly higher partial correlation (0.1355 vs 0.1307). Given identical context otherwise, the higher-coverage shrinkage model with marginally better partial-r is better supported than the much sparser penalized-regression sibling (PGS001823).

PGS002766 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for hypothyroidism because it provides a PRS-comparable effect size (OR per SD = 1.47, 95% CI 1.43–1.52) under basic covariate adjustment, whereas PGS005218 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.859) alongside heavy, disease-adjacent biomarker covariates (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) that likely inflate discrimination and are not comparable to PRS-only performance. Although PGS005218 has much larger multi-cohort training and validation and a disease-focused publication, its endpoint is incident hypothyroidism and its only visible metric is covariate-driven; PGS002766 has a cleaner endpoint label (hypothyroidism) and the only direct PRS signal reported in this head-to-head.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported match). However, PGS004911 is the more PRS-like genome-wide model (PRS-CS; 374,114 variants) with clean/basic covariates (age, sex, PCs) and reports PRS-relevant effect sizes (OR per SD 1.33; HR 2.34; plus high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9), whereas PGS000739 is a very sparse 27-variant GWS score whose reported AUROC (0.821) is from a heavily clinically augmented model including multiple clinical risk factors and rare-variant carrier status, making its full-model AUROC less informative about standalone PRS performance. With no PGS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the cleaner covariate design and stronger genome-wide PRS construction favor PGS004911 despite similar full-model AUROCs.

PGS005265 is better-supported for the target trait (hyperthyroidism) because its endpoint is Graves’ disease, which is a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a disease-focused multi-biobank study with broad external evaluation context (many contributing cohorts; EVAL MAE 100%) and a large validation sample (n=94,651). It also reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.63), which is meaningful PRS evidence even though only a full-model AUROC is shown (0.665) and covariates are unknown. In contrast, PGS001043 has exact label alignment (hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) and clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6323; R²=0.02158, below the heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet, 69 variants, UKB-only development), which is a systematic negative signal for external generalization versus a disease-focused multi-cohort score. Overall, the study archetype + strong effect size and dominant-subtype alignment favor PGS005265 despite weaker PRS-only metric reporting.

PGS005266 is better-supported for the target trait hyperthyroidism because its endpoint is Graves’ disease (the clinically dominant autoimmune form of hyperthyroidism) with coherent phenotype fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Graves’ disease) and it comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort biobank study with large external-style validation (n=94,651) and multi-ancestry evaluation context. Although it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.54), which is meaningful PRS signal. In contrast, PGS001043 is an exact-label hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis score but is from the known pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ sparse framework (snpnet, 69 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external generalization; its PRS-only metrics (AUROC 0.6323, R2 0.0216) are modest and not clearly decisive, even if they are clean and below the heritability ceiling. Overall, the disease-focused multi-cohort design plus strong effect-size evidence makes PGS005266 the stronger choice despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Genet paper with identical endpoint fidelity (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported both hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), identical ancestry context (EUR GWAS/EVAL), identical covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), identical development cohorts, and the same validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given that, PGS004911 has the only consistent empirical edge: it is the MTAG-enhanced version (explicitly preferred within-family per guidance) and it shows stronger reported performance/effect evidence in the selected record (higher full-model AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; higher R² 0.048 vs 0.031; slightly higher OR/HR). These differences are modest and full-model, hence Moderate confidence, but they favor PGS004911 over PGS004910.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS000739’s higher full-model AUROC (0.821 vs 0.73) is heavily discounted because its covariates include multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status (a strong non-PRS augmentation), making the metric less informative for standalone PRS quality. PGS004910 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, sex, PCs), reports supportive PRS effect sizes (e.g., HR 1.97; OR high vs median tertile 5.5), and is built with a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with far broader variant coverage (374,190 vs 27), which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease. Validation is also larger for PGS004910 (343,182 vs 184,511), though this is only a weak tie-break. Overall, PGS004910 is better-supported as a cleaner PRS rather than a clinically packaged predictor.

PGS000114 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its endpoint fidelity is an exact match at all key fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all JIA), whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with a different mapped EFO and phenotyping endpoint. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.738 vs 0.76) is not a reliable differentiator; instead, PGS000114 has stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR 2.085 vs 1.51) and a larger variant set (26 vs 12) under the same method (SparSNP) and similarly clean covariates (sex, PCs) and ancestry context (EUR-only).

PGS005218 is better supported overall: it is from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with much broader multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) and a far larger evaluation sample (n=441,692) than PGS004935 (UKB-only development; eval n=8,417). Although both candidates only report full-model AUROC (no PRS-only AUC/R2), PGS005218’s reported AUROC=0.859 is heavily confounded by explicit thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making it non-comparable as PRS evidence; however PGS004935’s AUROC=0.7 is also full-model and its covariates are unknown, so it is not cleaner on metric comparability. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both, but PGS005218’s phenotyping is explicitly incident hypothyroidism and its genome-wide shrinkage approach with very large variant count (1,110,091; PRS-CS) is structurally stronger than the sparse SnpNet score (6,127 variants) from a portability-style paper. Net: stronger study archetype + broader development/validation context outweigh PGS004935’s lone OR=1.5 effect-size field.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to hypothyroidism (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both are EUR-only in development/evaluation, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported. PGS004935’s only discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.7 (not PRS-comparable) with covariates listed as Unknown, so its apparent performance advantage is not interpretable as PRS strength. PGS002766, while lacking AUC/R2, reports a very similar per-SD OR (1.47 vs 1.5) and has explicitly basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), which is cleaner/less ambiguous for PRS evaluation than unknown covariate handling. Given the absence of PRS-only metrics for both, the clearer covariate specification and comparable effect size make PGS002766 better-supported overall.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported kidney cancer; trait_efo renal cell carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer), identical ancestry context (EUR GWAS/EVAL), identical covariates, identical variant count (19), and essentially identical full-model discrimination/effect sizes (AUROC ~0.722; C-index ~0.723–0.724; HR per SD ~1.15–1.16). However, PGS000787 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000076 (“19 variants from Graff et al (PGS000076) with inverse variant weights”), which is a strong negative support signal versus the original, correctly oriented score. The extra R² reported for PGS000787 (0.366) is not labeled PRS-only and is implausible relative to the provided kidney-cancer heritability ceiling (h2_liability ~0.0178), suggesting it is not a comparable PRS metric and should not outweigh the provenance issue. Therefore the better-supported record is the original PGS000076.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it is disease-focused (kidney-cancer GWAS meta-analysis identifying susceptibility regions) with direct endpoint alignment (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Kidney cancer”) and shows a much stronger PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.5 [1.43–1.58]) than PGS000076 (HR 1.16 [1.08–1.26]), suggesting materially stronger genetic discrimination. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 and only report full-model AUROC (0.74 vs 0.722), which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric and the small AUROC gap is not decisive; covariate sets are similarly epidemiologic (age/sex/PCs plus BMI/smoking/hypertension). PGS000076 has an incident-only endpoint and comes from a cross-cancer evaluation framework with fewer variants (19 vs 107), offering weaker PRS signal despite a slightly larger validation N. Overall, PGS004908 has the stronger disease-specific evidence package and effect-size support.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (N18 chronic renal failure mapped to kidney failure), ancestry (EUR dev/eval), cohorts (UKB), training size (n=174,489), validation size (n=56,192), and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2. Method differences (metaPRS vs LDpred2) are secondary here, but are directionally consistent with multi-score aggregation being a positive structural signal.

PGS004562 has better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is directly “N18 (Chronic renal failure)”, which aligns with kidney failure, whereas PGS000708’s phenotyping_reported is explicitly restricted to “Diabetic kidney failure in all” (a subtype/etiology-specific endpoint). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be compared on clean PRS metrics; in that setting, PGS004562 also shows a stronger per-SD effect size signal (OR=1.395) than PGS000708 (HR=1.19), while both are EUR-only UKB-based. PGS000708 has cleaner disclosed basic covariates and larger validation, but those advantages don’t outweigh its narrower diabetic-only phenotype for a generic kidney failure target.

PGS002767 is the better-supported standalone knee osteoarthritis PRS on the visible fields: it has direct endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Knee osteoarthritis”) and transparent basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), avoiding risk-factor/packaging ambiguity. PGS004549 maps to the same EFO but is explicitly a risk-factor–integrated metaPRS (“Integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”), with unknown covariates and a coded phenotype label (M17 gonarthrosis) that is compatible but less directly aligned to the target wording. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, and their per-SD ORs are similar (~1.35 vs ~1.37), so the decision rests mainly on endpoint clarity and lower leakage risk, favoring PGS002767.

Both candidates map cleanly to knee osteoarthritis (same trait_efo), but PGS002729 has higher endpoint fidelity and clearer evaluation evidence: it is explicitly a knee osteoarthritis PRS with clinical osteoarthritis phenotyping, multi-cohort disease-focused development (BBJ/UKB/arcOGEN/deCODE etc.), and a reported AUROC (0.66, albeit full-model with age/sex/BMI). In contrast, PGS004549 is a risk-factor–integrated metaPRS framework score (title indicates integration of risk-factor PRS with disease PRS), with unknown covariates and no discrimination metrics reported (only an OR=1.37), making its standalone PRS evidence and comparability weaker despite larger variant count and larger validation N.

PGS002767 is the better-supported standalone PRS for the target knee osteoarthritis: it has exact endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported = "Knee osteoarthritis" matching trait_reported/trait_efo) and provides a PRS-discriminative effect size (OR per SD 1.35, moderate signal) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS; 1,052,275 variants) consistent with a polygenic architecture. PGS002729, while disease-focused and listing multiple development cohorts, has weaker endpoint specificity (phenotyping_reported = "Clinical osteoarthritis" rather than knee-specific) and its only visible discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.66 with covariates including BMI (not PRS-only and not directly comparable), plus a very sparse 24-variant GWS score that is structurally less likely to capture polygenic signal. With both lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, the cleaner knee-specific endpoint and stronger genome-wide PRS structure tip the decision to PGS002767.

PGS000708 has better endpoint fidelity and clearer evaluation context for the target trait: it is explicitly mapped and reported as “Kidney failure” with a specified phenotype (“Diabetic kidney failure in all”) and disclosed basic covariates (age as time scale, sex, batch, PCs), plus a representative discrimination metric (full-model C-index 0.779) and HR with CI.
