PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” on endpoint fidelity and disease-focused evidence: it directly targets kidney cancer (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Kidney cancer”) and comes from a dedicated kidney-cancer multi-ancestry GWAS identifying susceptibility regions, with a much stronger PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.5, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) and a larger, clean EUR evaluation sample (n=324,805). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the stronger disease-specific design plus stronger effect size favors PGS004908.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo is late-onset Alzheimer’s disease; phenotyping_reported is late-onset AD), and neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R². Both candidates match the target trait well (lung cancer/lung carcinoma) with identical endpoint fidelity (incident lung cancer), identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical covariate bundle (including smoking variables and family history), and essentially identical reported full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849) and similar HR per SD (1.16 vs 1.17). With no PRS-only AUC/R² for either, the original disease score (PGS000078) is better-supported than the inverted-weight derivative (PGS000789).

PGS000754 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is a clean direct SLE diagnosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to systemic lupus erythematosus), whereas PGS000196’s phenotyping is explicitly conditioned on an arthritis outpatient context (“SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis”), which is a narrower, potentially packaged clinical setting. Both candidates are near-clones: same target (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease), same phenotyping_reported (familial LOAD), same method (21 genome-wide significant variants), same covariates (age, sex), same publication and development cohorts, and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2. Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo lymphoid leukemia; phenotyping_reported Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), with EUR-only evaluation and the same validation sample size (n=391,338). PGS000754 is the better-supported match to the generic target trait “lupus erythematosus” because its phenotyping_reported is an unrestricted systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosis, whereas PGS000328 is explicitly restricted to early-onset SLE (onset before age 20), a subtype/age-conditioned endpoint that is a poorer fit for general lupus risk. Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. PGS000789 is heavily packaged with non-genetic risk factors (family history, PM2.5, detailed smoking intensity/duration plus interaction terms), making its high full-model AUROC/C-index largely covariate-driven and less informative about standalone PRS quality. Given similar endpoint fidelity and ancestry (EUR-only), the cleaner packaging plus stronger method/variant architecture makes PGS004860 better-supported overall.

Both candidates match the target trait well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease in trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported). Both candidates map cleanly to systemic lupus erythematosus (same trait_reported and trait_efo) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.83 for PGS000328 vs 0.79 for PGS000196) are not strong, PRS-comparable differentiators. Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are all lung cancer / incident lung cancer; EUR GWAS and EUR evaluation). Both candidates target the exact same endpoint (age-related macular degeneration) with identical phenotyping_reported and the same basic covariates (age, sex, PCs 1–10), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not directly comparable as a standalone PRS metric). PGS000077 is better supported for the target trait (lymphoid leukemia) because its endpoint is a clear incident lymphocytic leukemia diagnosis and it comes from a multi-cohort cross-cancer evaluation with very large European evaluation (n=391,338) and a reasonably strong per-SD effect size (HR=1.45). PGS000788 is better supported for the target lymphoid leukemia because its endpoint fidelity is strong and explicit (phenotyping_reported: incident lymphocytic leukemia; trait_efo matches), it uses a substantially richer PRS (75 variants vs 6 for PGS000645), and it shows a strong PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.7) under basic covariate adjustment (age/sex/PCs/array), suggesting meaningful genetic signal even though only full-model AUROC is reported. PGS000645 has an exact generic label match but is extremely sparse (6 variants), has weaker overall discrimination evidence (full-model AUROC 0.578; modest OR per SD 1.358), and is developed in a single cohort (MGI) with small training n=1,100, offering less robust support than the multi-cohort-derived score used in PGS000788.

Both candidates align to the target trait at the concept level (trait_reported/efo = age-related macular degeneration) and both are EUR-trained/EUR-evaluated with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS004952 adds survey membership but no heavy clinical leakage). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS004952 (0.842) is not a reliable PRS-comparable advantage, especially given a likely formatting inconsistency in classification_metrics (AUROC shown as 84.2). With PRS-only metrics absent, structural and effect-size evidence dominate: PGS004606 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1,000,946 variants and shows a much stronger per-SD OR (1.76 vs 1.41 for PGS004952), indicating stronger standalone genetic discrimination. PGS004606 also has far larger validation (n=163,011 vs n=1,232), which mildly supports robustness. Overall, PGS004606 is better-supported as a PRS for macular degeneration, while PGS004952’s apparent AUROC edge is full-model and less comparable.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma), use the same method (genome-wide significant variants) and same variant count (23), and are EUR-only in GWAS and evaluation—so phenotype and structural signals do not differentiate. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC difference (0.69 in PGS002306 vs 0.644 in PGS002281) is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage, especially with PGS002306 having unknown covariates. PGS002281 provides clearer evaluation context (covariates explicitly age/sex/region) and includes a meaningful PRS-stratification effect size (OR 3.18 highest vs lowest quintile), which PGS002306 lacks. Given the near-clone nature, the better-supported covariate transparency plus additional effect-size evidence makes PGS002281 the stronger record.

Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication and release date, same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), identical ancestry distributions, and same validation sample size (n=30,379). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; only full-model C-index is shown and is essentially indistinguishable. With metrics largely non-comparable for PRS ranking, the only visible differentiators slightly favor PGS005039: marginally higher full-model C-index (0.78484 vs 0.78385) and slightly stronger OR per SD (1.578 vs 1.554). Given the tiny differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is low.

PGS002247 is better supported for the target melanoma endpoint because its phenotyping is explicitly aligned to a clean clinical outcome (“Incident invasive melanoma”) and its reported performance is based on a relatively light covariate set (age, sex), making the full-model AUROC/R² less likely to be dominated by non-genetic risk packaging. In contrast, PGS000743 reports a higher full-model AUROC (0.74 vs 0.691) but uses an extensive bundle of traditional risk factors including family history and keratinocyte cancer personal history, which strongly inflates and reduces comparability of the AUROC to PRS quality; neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R² to isolate genetic contribution. With similar method family and ancestry (EUR-only) and no PRS-only metrics, the cleaner endpoint/covariate design in PGS002247 outweighs PGS000743’s covariate-heavy AUROC advantage.

PGS004607 is better supported as a standalone PRS for macular degeneration because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (1,067,520) and shows a slightly stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.48 vs 1.41 for PGS004952), which is a more PRS-informative signal than full-model AUROC when PRS-only metrics are absent. Both candidates match the target trait at the EFO level, but PGS004952’s phenotyping is explicitly restricted to “Late” AMD under a specific clinical classification system, making it a narrower endpoint than PGS004607’s general “Age-related macular degeneration.” The much higher full-model AUROC reported for PGS004952 (0.842) is not PRS-comparable (no PGS-only/incremental metrics) and is therefore discounted, especially given similar basic covariates in both. Despite PGS004607’s ancestry mismatch (AFR GWAS, EUR evaluation), its overall PRS construction evidence and endpoint generality outweigh PGS004952’s sparse 52-SNP GWS score and non-comparable AUROC advantage.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to multiple myeloma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and both are EUR-only evaluations with only basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly comparable; still, PGS002281 shows materially stronger validation evidence (full-model AUROC 0.644 vs 0.577 for PGS000653) and a stronger stratification effect (OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18 vs OR top 1% vs rest 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1 for PGS000653). Variant counts and methods are near-identical (23 vs 22 GWAS-hit style), and validation N is similar, so the performance/effect-size edge favors PGS002281 despite PGS000653 having an explicit training sample and UKB development cohort listed.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical endpoint fidelity (MI PheCode 411.2; trait_efo myocardial infarction; phenotyping_reported myocardial infarction), same publication, same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With endpoints and design effectively tied, the only differentiators are marginally stronger reported performance/effect size for candidate_b (PGS005045: full-model C-index 0.78385; OR 1.554) versus candidate_a (PGS005035: 0.78336; OR 1.541). These differences are small and based on full-model metrics, so confidence is low, but PGS005045 has the slight edge on the available evidence.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative. PGS002726 has stronger PRS signal evidence via a much larger variant set (476,399 vs 127) and a markedly stronger stratification effect size (OR top 10% vs median = 15.0) compared with PGS000809’s modest variance explained (R²=0.069) and beta without a clear PRS-only context. Although PGS000809 has a larger validation sample (8,370 vs 938) and explicitly basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), the small full-model AUROC difference (0.765 vs 0.8) is not decisive and PGS002726’s effect-size/structure package is more supportive of a stronger standalone MS PRS.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/EFO (melanoma), identical endpoint fidelity (incident invasive melanoma), same basic covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same publication and validation sample size (n=4,765), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R², which are not clean PRS-comparable). With endpoints and design effectively tied, the remaining differentiators are small full-model metric differences and structural signals: PGS002247 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.691 vs 0.688) and R² (0.072 vs 0.070) and includes more genome-wide significant variants (68 vs 50), which is a modest within-method advantage. The evidence gap is small, so confidence is moderate rather than high.

Both candidates are EUR-only GWAS/evaluation, use the same method family (genome-wide significant variants), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R²—so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable PRS metrics. PGS000743’s higher full-model AUROC (0.74) is heavily discounted because it is paired with an extensive covariate set including family history and multiple traditional risk factors, making the discrimination likely covariate-driven and less informative about the PRS itself. PGS002246 uses only age and sex covariates and has a more endpoint-faithful, clinically specific phenotyping description (“incident invasive melanoma”), making its reported performance less confounded by clinical risk-factor packaging. Variant counts and ancestry are similar (50 vs 45 SNPs; EUR/EUR), so covariate/endpoint fidelity drives the decision in favor of PGS002246.

Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same method (ldpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distributions, and same validation size (n=30,379), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either (only full-model C-index). With design essentially identical, the only differentiators are slightly stronger reported performance/effect size for PGS005039 (full-model C-index 0.7848 vs 0.7834; OR per SD 1.578 vs 1.541), so PGS005039 edges out PGS005035, but the margin is minimal.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple sclerosis). PGS001270 has clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6586; PGS-only R2 0.0290, below the h2_liability ceiling 0.1174) and basic covariates, but it comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse 41-variant snpnet model—an archetype that domain guidance flags as typically underperforming disease-focused scores in external validation. PGS002726 is from a disease-focused MS susceptibility/phenotype study (IMSGC; Brain) and shows strong MS risk stratification (OR top 10% vs median = 15.0), which is meaningful PRS signal even though only a full-model AUROC (0.80) is reported and PRS-only AUC/R2 are missing. Given the framework penalty and sparse architecture of PGS001270 versus the disease-focused evidence and strong effect size for PGS002726, PGS002726 is better-supported overall, with moderate confidence due to the lack of PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for the target trait (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported J33 nasal polyp; trait_efo Nasal Cavity Polyp), come from the same publication, and have the same EUR-only training/validation context (UKB; n=174,489 train; n=56,192 eval) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, so performance metrics cannot differentiate. The main differentiator is the available PRS-discrimination proxy: PGS004535 reports a materially stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.60) than PGS004465 (OR=1.35), which is meaningful evidence of stronger PRS signal when AUC/R2 are missing. Method-wise, PGS004535 is also a multi-score aggregation/meta-PRS (RFDiseasemetaPRS) versus the single-score LDpred2 in PGS004465, which is a positive structural signal when other fields are tied.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate multiple sclerosis) and both use only basic covariates. However, PGS001270 is from a known pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper ("across 813 traits"), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external generalization despite clean PRS-only metrics; its PRS-only AUROC/R2 are modest (0.659/0.029). PGS000809 comes from a disease-focused MS study with multi-cohort development (IMSGC/WTCCC etc.) and a larger variant set (127 vs 41), which is stronger study-archetype support for an MS-specific PRS even though it reports only full-model metrics (AUROC 0.765) rather than PRS-only. Given the framework penalty on PGS001270 and the disease-focused multi-cohort evidence for PGS000809, PGS000809 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Tobacco use disorder; trait_efo: nicotine dependence), come from the same UKB portability paper, have identical training size (n=391,124), similar multi-ancestry evaluation, identical covariates, and the same validation sample size (n=19,400), so endpoint fidelity and study context do not differentiate them. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the best available comparable metric is partial correlation: PGS002037 is higher (partial-r 0.0741, CI 0.0601–0.0881) than PGS001830 (0.0557, CI 0.0416–0.0697). Structurally, PGS002037 also uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (847,691 vs 13,838), which is a positive signal for a polygenic trait when other fields are matched. Therefore PGS002037 is better supported than PGS001830 on the visible evidence.

Both candidates match the target trait equally well (same trait_reported/trait_efo and same phenotyping_reported) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.5876 in PGS005263 vs 0.5854 in PGS005261) are essentially non-decisive. On structural and supportive evidence, PGS005263 is stronger: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a materially larger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.36, β≈0.309) than PGS005261’s sparse P+T score with 110 variants and weak effect size (OR≈1.05, β≈0.047). Validation sample size and evaluation ancestry are the same, and PGS005261’s slightly broader cohort list does not outweigh the method/variant-count/effect-size advantage of PGS005263.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/trait_efo and same phenotyping_reported string), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry distribution (MAE 100%), and same validation sample size (n=94,651), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With endpoint fidelity and study context essentially identical, the best available differentiator is the slightly stronger empirical signal in candidate_a: higher full-model AUROC (0.5933 vs 0.5876) and higher per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.408 vs 1.362; β 0.342 vs 0.309). Candidate_b has a slightly smaller cohort list and slightly fewer variants, offering no compensating advantage. Therefore PGS005262 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical aside from a typo), come from the same publication and cohorts, and have the same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size, so endpoint fidelity and transportability do not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference is weak evidence, but PGS005262 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.593 vs 0.585) and—more importantly—much stronger PRS signal in effect sizes (OR per SD 1.41, β 0.34) versus PGS005261 (OR 1.05, β 0.047), consistent with better standalone discrimination. Structurally, PGS005262 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants versus a very sparse P+T score with 110 variants in PGS005261, which is a favorable tie-break for a polygenic disease trait.

PGS005235 is better supported for the target trait obesity because its endpoint fidelity is explicitly anchored to an obesity diagnosis phecode (phenotyping_reported: "Obesity (phecode: 278.1)") despite the broader trait_reported label ("Adiposity"), and it comes from a multi-cohort development context (EGG, GIANT, UKB) with clearly stated basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs), reducing concerns about hidden clinical-risk packaging. Both candidates lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so effect-size evidence becomes more important; PGS005235 reports a substantially stronger OR (1.97) than PGS004447 (1.36). PGS004447 has an exact ICD10 label (E66) and more variants, but it is from a risk-factor integration paper with unknown covariates, which weakens comparability and interpretability versus PGS005235’s clearer, diagnosis-anchored phenotype and cleaner covariate disclosure.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to multiple myeloma (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported) and both are sparse GWAS-hit style scores with similar variant counts (PGS002306: 23 vs PGS000653: 22) in EUR-only GWAS/EVAL. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS002306 (0.69) is not a reliable PRS-comparable advantage, especially with covariates listed as Unknown. PGS000653 provides a more interpretable and better-documented evidence package: explicit basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), a stated training sample size (n=3,377) and cohort (UKB), plus additional performance evidence beyond AUROC (Nagelkerke R²=0.0145, OR per SD=1.327 with CI). Given comparable phenotype alignment and method, the clearer covariate/metric documentation and effect-size reporting make PGS000653 better-supported overall.

PGS004447 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target trait obesity: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly ICD10 E66 (Obesity) with trait_efo=obesity, whereas PGS002033 uses a broader administrative bundle (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”) and maps to multiple EFO concepts (obesity/overweight/overnutrition), making it less specific to obesity. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics don’t separate them; however PGS004447 provides a moderate per-SD effect size (OR≈1.36) as direct PRS signal, while PGS002033 only reports a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.079) and comes from a portability-style framework paper. Although PGS002033 has larger training N and multi-ancestry evaluation plus explicit basic covariates, those are secondary to endpoint specificity here, so PGS004447 is better-supported for obesity.

PGS001273 is the better match to the generic target trait “osteoporosis” because its endpoint is directly osteoporosis in both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS001274 is explicitly a narrower subtype/time-to-event definition (“osteoporosis without pathological fracture (time-to-event)”), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic osteoporosis target. Both candidates come from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper, with identical training cohort (UKB), training N, covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size, so design/transportability do not differentiate them. Although PGS001274 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC/R2 and more variants, those gains are modest and do not outweigh the cleaner phenotype alignment of PGS001273 for the stated target; hence the choice is close and confidence is low.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Osteoporosis). However, PGS001273 is from a clear pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (316 variants) with weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.5685; PGS-only R2 0.00688), and its high full-model AUROC (0.7897) is largely covariate-driven given the tiny incremental AUROC (0.00477). PGS002768, while lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, comes from a disease-comparative study context (family history vs PRS across diseases) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (~1.09M) and a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.38) in a larger EUR validation (n=39,444 vs 24,905). Given the framework penalty and weak PRS-only metrics for PGS001273, PGS002768 is better-supported overall despite missing AUC/R2.

PGS000082 better matches the generic target concept (ovarian neoplasm) via a direct disease endpoint (“Incident ovarian cancer”), whereas PGS003394 is packaged as horizon-specific prediction (“10-year ovarian cancer risks”), which domain guidance flags as absolute-risk/risk-wrapper packaging and a negative for standalone PRS comparability. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model C-index difference (0.656 in PGS000082 vs 0.623 in PGS003394) is not a clean differentiator, especially given PGS000082’s explicitly heavy covariate set (including family history) and PGS003394’s unknown covariates. PGS003394 has some multi-ancestry evaluation, but its selected validation ancestry is still European and the endpoint packaging concern remains; overall PGS000082 has the cleaner disease-status phenotype alignment for the target.

PGS005235 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target obesity: despite the broader trait_reported (“Adiposity”), its phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Obesity (phecode: 278.1)” and trait_efo is obesity, indicating a direct diagnosis-anchored endpoint. It also shows stronger PRS signal evidence via an OR≈1.97 per SD, which is a strong discriminative indicator when PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. In contrast, PGS002033 comes from a UKB portability/framework-style paper (“Portability of 245 polygenic scores…”) with a broader administrative phenotype label (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”) and only a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.079) as performance evidence; while it has multi-ancestry evaluation, that does not outweigh the weaker endpoint specificity and weaker PRS-signal metric. Both have only basic covariates and lack clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so the decision rests mainly on endpoint fidelity and strength of available PRS evidence, favoring PGS005235.

PGS002046 is the better-supported choice on structural and endpoint grounds: it targets plain otosclerosis with a direct diagnosis phenotype (“Otosclerosis”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (570,308), plus a broader multi-ancestry evaluation mix (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS) consistent with a portability/transferability assessment. PGS001255, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6319; PGS-only R2 0.01341, plausibly below the heritability ceiling), is explicitly a time-to-event endpoint (“TTE otosclerosis”) from the sparse pan-trait UKB snpnet framework with only 213 variants—an archetype that domain guidance flags as less reliable for external generalization. Confidence is low because PGS002046 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so the decision rests mainly on endpoint fidelity and method/coverage rather than directly comparable performance.

Both candidates align well to the target (ovarian neoplasm) with identical trait_reported/trait_efo and the same endpoint (phenotyping_reported: incident ovarian cancer), same EUR-only evaluation, same variant count (36), and essentially identical covariate set (including family history), so full-model AUROC differences (0.656 in PGS000082 vs 0.66 in PGS000793) are not meaningful and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS000793 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000082 (“36 variants from Graff et al (PGS000082) with inverse variant weights”), which is a structural red flag versus the original, and its reported R² (0.193) appears to be full-model/variance-explained rather than PRS-only and thus not a clean advantage. Given near-clone design and metrics, the original directly specified GWAS-hits score (PGS000082) is better-supported than an inversely weighted reparameterization (PGS000793).

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident pancreatic cancer), have identical variant count (22), ancestry evaluation (EUR), covariates (including family history and smoking/BMI), and essentially identical reported discrimination/effect size (full-model AUROC ~0.745; C-index ~0.742–0.743; HR per SD ~1.49). However, PGS000794 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000083 with inverse variant weights, which is a strong warning for endpoint-faithful PRS quality (directionality likely incorrect) and provides no compensating PRS-only metrics. The extra R² reported for PGS000794 appears to be full-model/other-metric (not PRS-only) and is not a reliable advantage. Therefore the original, non-inverted score PGS000083 is better-supported.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a clean differentiator. PGS000663 is from a pancreatic-cancer–focused risk prediction study and is evaluated in a more ancestry-diverse setting (EAS 33%, EUR 67%), which is supportive for transportability, whereas PGS000794 comes from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration paper with a very large EUR-only evaluation and covariates including family history of cancer that can inflate full-model metrics. Effect sizes are similar (PGS000794 HR 1.49 vs PGS000663 OR 1.44), so the study archetype/packaging and broader evaluation ancestry tilt the balance toward PGS000663.

PGS002768 is the better-supported choice for generic osteoporosis risk because its endpoint is a direct osteoporosis phenotype (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Osteoporosis”) and it comes from a disease-comparative but not pan-trait UKB sweep, using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (1,091,549) and a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.38) under basic covariates. In contrast, PGS001274 is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse snpnet framework (a negative archetype for external generalization) and uses a time-to-event, subtype-like endpoint (“osteoporosis without pathological fracture (TTE)”), which is less faithful to the broad target trait; although it reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (AUROC≈0.576, R2≈0.009), these are modest and do not outweigh the framework + TTE endpoint penalties versus the more disease-aligned, genome-wide PRS-CS score.

PGS000793 is better aligned to the generic target “ovarian neoplasm” via a direct disease endpoint (“Incident ovarian cancer”) without horizon-conditioned risk packaging, whereas PGS003394’s phenotyping is explicitly “10-year ovarian cancer risks,” which is a deployment-style, horizon-conditioned formulation that domain guidance flags as negative evidence for standalone PRS quality/comparability. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the small full-model discrimination difference (0.66 vs 0.623 C-index) is not a reliable differentiator, especially given PGS000793’s heavy covariate set (including family history) and PGS003394’s unknown covariates. With metrics largely non-comparable, endpoint fidelity favors PGS000793, but confidence is low because both are epithelial/ovarian carcinoma-aligned and both lack clean PRS-only performance.

Both candidates target the same disease concept (trait_reported pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and use the same sparse GWAS-hits construction (22 genome-wide significant variants), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either record—so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator. Given that, PGS000083 has the stronger overall support: it uses a straightforward incident pancreatic cancer endpoint (vs PGS000663’s horizon-conditioned 0–10 years follow-up packaging) and shows stronger reported discrimination/effect evidence in its selected record (full-model AUROC 0.745 with C-index 0.742 and HR 1.49) compared with PGS000663 (full-model AUROC 0.67 and OR 1.44). PGS000083 also has far broader validation scale (n=391,491 vs n=956), while PGS000663’s covariates include additional clinical factors (e.g., diabetic status, waist-to-hip ratio, fasting/month-year collection) that further reduce comparability of its full-model AUROC.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Parkinson’s disease) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not a reliable differentiator—especially because PGS001774’s AUROC=0.80 is from a covariate-heavy risk-factor package including family history and other exposures, making it less comparable to standalone PRS performance. PGS000903 is better-supported as a disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis-derived PRS with far richer genetic content (1805 variants vs 12) and includes PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25; beta reported) with cleaner/basic covariates (PCs, age, sex). Overall, PGS000903 has stronger structural and study-archetype support, while PGS001774 looks more like an integrated clinical risk model where the reported AUROC is likely covariate-driven.

PGS000325 is the better-supported choice for the broad target of juvenile idiopathic arthritis because, while both candidates are subtype-specific JIA scores from the same disease-focused publication with identical ancestry context (EUR-only), cohorts, and similarly basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), PGS000325 shows consistently stronger performance evidence: higher reported AUROC (0.80 vs 0.76) and a materially stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.93 vs 1.51). Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so the tie-break relies on effect size and within-family discrimination, where PGS000325 is clearly stronger. PGS000326 is similarly well-aligned but has weaker discrimination/effect size and slightly fewer variants (12 vs 21), offering less support.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept despite not reporting PRS-only AUC/R2: it targets a clinically specific and closely aligned endpoint (trait_reported Peripheral artery disease; phenotyping_reported incident PAD) and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort study with broad external multi-ancestry evaluation (validation n=304,294 across AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS) and a strong PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.66). In contrast, PGS002055 is from a UKB portability framework paper with a vaguer phenotype (“peripheral vascular disease, unspecified”), much smaller validation (n=19,668), and only a very weak PRS-comparable signal (partial-r 0.0175) with no effect-size support. Both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint fidelity + disease-focused evidence package favors PGS005217.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Parkinson’s disease) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROCs are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. However, PGS001774’s high full-model AUROC=0.80 is paired with a covariate set that includes family history and multiple established risk factors (head injury, depression, smoking, BMI), making the reported discrimination likely heavily covariate-driven and less informative about standalone PRS quality. In contrast, PGS000902 is a disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis score using only basic covariates (PCs, age, sex) and has a much richer genetic model (90 variants vs 12), with clearer large-scale consortium-style development context. Given the reduced leakage risk and stronger disease-GWAS-derived PRS construction, PGS000902 is better supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all prostate cancer), study context (same publication, UKB training, same ancestry distribution, same validation N=171,474), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R² (so full-model AUROC/R² are only weak tie-breakers). Given that, PGS004155 is better-supported because it shows consistently stronger reported performance in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.7049 vs 0.7003; R² 0.1280 vs 0.1213) and slightly stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 2.166 vs 2.109; β 0.773 vs 0.746), while PGS004139 has no compensating advantage on endpoint, covariates, ancestry, or validation breadth.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept despite a slight label mismatch (peripheral artery disease vs peripheral vascular disease): its phenotyping is a clear clinical endpoint (“Incident peripheral artery disease”), it comes from a disease-focused PAD/MALE study (JAMA Cardiol) with broad multi-cohort development and large multi-ancestry evaluation (n=304,294), and it reports a strong PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.66). PGS003587 is better supported for the target trait preeclampsia because its endpoint evidence is more coherent: although trait_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” both trait_efo is preeclampsia and phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia,” aligning directly to the target. Confidence is Moderate because both come from framework/portability-style UKB papers and PGS001312’s PGS-only R2 appears high relative to the provided local heritability sanity-check, which adds some uncertainty.

PGS001313 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence for psoriasis: it reports clean PGS-only AUROC (0.6729, with CI) and PGS-only R² (0.04966) under basic covariates, whereas PGS002083 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0632) and no PRS-only AUROC/R², making cross-model discrimination evidence weaker and less directly comparable. PGS003861 is a disease-focused pulmonary embolism score with direct endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Pulmonary embolism”) and is developed/validated in a coherent single-population context (Han Chinese; GWAS+EVAL EAS 100%), plus it reports a strong risk stratification effect size (OR 5.08 for quantile contrast). PGS001280 is the better-supported match to the target trait pulmonary embolism: its trait_efo is specific to pulmonary embolism and its reported phenotype is PE time-to-event, whereas PGS001279 is a broader/combined mapping (trait_efo includes pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis) and is framed as “previously: Blood clot in the lung,” which is less cleanly PE-specific. Given that, the best differentiator is the observed validation signal: PGS000471 shows materially stronger full-model AUROC (0.569 vs 0.524), higher pseudo-R² (0.0255 vs 0.00141), stronger OR per SD (1.401 vs 1.09), and much higher top-1% vs rest OR (3.77 vs 1.48). PGS000469’s much larger variant count and PRS-CS method do not overcome its consistently weaker reported discrimination/effect-size evidence in this same-study, same-endpoint comparison.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to squamous cell carcinoma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.605 for PGS000731 vs 0.589 for PGS000465) are not decisive and are not PRS-comparable. PGS000465 has cleaner, explicitly stated basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4) and provides richer performance evidence beyond AUROC (Nagelkerke R², Brier score, and a strong top-1% vs rest OR=4.54), whereas PGS000731 has covariates listed as unknown and offers less interpretable performance detail (only full-model AUROC and a per-SD OR). Despite PGS000731’s larger validation sample and slightly higher full-model AUROC, PGS000465 is better-supported on-record due to clearer evaluation specification and more informative metrics.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Squamous cell carcinoma”) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. PGS000731 is better supported by substantially larger external evaluation (n=88,924 vs n=8,473 for PGS000461) and comes from a disease-focused skin cancer risk score study, whereas PGS000461 is from a repository-style Cancer PRSweb framework context with a very small GWAS-hits score (13 variants) and modest validation. While PGS000461 has cleaner disclosed basic covariates and a slightly higher per-SD OR (1.49 vs 1.44), the effect-size gap is small and does not outweigh PGS000731’s much broader validation support and comparable endpoint fidelity.

PGS000014 is better supported for generic type 2 diabetes risk because it provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only/PRS R2=0.029) with basic covariate adjustment and a very large validation sample (n=288,978) plus broad multi-ancestry evaluation. PGS002243 has similar trait mapping but is incident/time-to-event framed ("Incident type 2 diabetes") and reports only a full-model C-index (0.741) plus HR=1.64 without any PRS-only AUC/R2, making its discrimination evidence less directly comparable for PRS quality. Training size and method are similar (both LDpred, genome-wide), so the decisive advantage is PGS000014’s explicit PRS-only R2 and broader evaluation context.

Both candidates match the target trait (T1D; EFO type 1 diabetes mellitus) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model discrimination is not directly comparable as PRS evidence. PGS004162 has better endpoint fidelity for a generic T1D target (phenotyping_reported="T1D" vs PGS004874 "Incident T1D" time-to-event framing) and a cleaner covariate profile (covariates="0" vs PCs 1–10), reducing risk that reported metrics are covariate-driven. It also shows stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 2.89 vs HR 2.37) and uses an ensemble-style method (MultiPRS) which is a positive structural signal versus a single-score MegaPRS. Although PGS004874 has much larger validation N and similar full-model C-index (~0.77), those are weak tie-breakers given the endpoint/covariate and effect-size advantages for PGS004162.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are T1D). However, PGS001297 is from a known pan-trait UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”), with a very sparse 69-variant snpnet model—an archetype that domain guidance flags as often less reliable in external transport despite clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 reporting (PGS-only R2=0.0912, AUROC=0.771). PGS004162 comes from a biobank evaluation/ensemble-learning study and uses a multi-score/ensemble-style method (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) with far broader genome coverage (62,645 variants) and a much larger validation sample (n=90,274) with some non-EUR evaluation (EUR/SAS), plus strong effect-size evidence (OR per SD ~2.89). Although PGS004162 lacks explicit PGS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics shown), its study archetype and ensemble structure provide stronger overall support than the sparse pan-trait framework score.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all thyroid cancer/thyroid carcinoma), same method (GWAS Hits) with the same 10 variants, and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either. With endpoint and design essentially matched, PGS000631 has consistently stronger reported validation signals in the selected European evaluation: higher full-model AUROC (0.636 vs 0.626), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0478 vs 0.0393), and stronger effect sizes/stratification (OR per SD 1.651 vs 1.598; top 1% vs rest OR 4.4 vs 3.53). PGS000630’s only notable advantage is larger training/validation size and a mixed-ancestry evaluation (EUR+MAE), but validation size is a weak tie-break and the mixed evaluation doesn’t outweigh the stronger performance/effect-size evidence for PGS000631.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate T2D) and both use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; no family history/biomarker/risk-calculator packaging). The key differentiator is PRS-comparable performance evidence: PGS000014 reports a clean PRS-only Nagelkerke R²=0.029 (and overall R²=0.029), which is directly interpretable and plausibly below the T2D heritability ceiling, whereas PGS002308 reports only full-model AUROC=0.793 and R²=0.092 without PRS-only metrics, making its apparent performance advantage non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven. Although PGS002308 is explicitly trans-ancestry and reports a strong OR=1.96 with diverse evaluation ancestries, the lack of PRS-only metrics and missing training sample details leave weaker directly comparable support than PGS000014’s explicit PRS-only R² plus large, multi-ancestry evaluation.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Thyroid cancer” / thyroid carcinoma), come from the same publication, use the same training cohort (MGI) with identical training (n=4,481), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and validation sample size (n=4,270), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. In this near-clone setting, PGS000630 has slightly stronger overall discrimination evidence (full-model AUROC 0.626 vs 0.618; Nagelkerke R² 0.0393 vs 0.0365; OR per SD 1.598 vs 1.568), and it also has broader evaluation ancestry (EUR+MAE) than PGS000632 (EUR only), which is mildly supportive for transportability. PGS000632’s higher top-1% OR (5.14 vs 3.53) is a positive signal but not enough to outweigh the consistently slightly better overall metrics and broader eval context of PGS000630.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to thyroid carcinoma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Thyroid cancer”), from the same publication, with similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4) and EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. Given that, PGS000631 has slightly stronger observed validation signals (higher full-model AUROC 0.636 vs 0.618; higher Nagelkerke R² 0.0478 vs 0.0365; higher per-SD OR 1.651 vs 1.568), while PGS000632’s main advantages are larger training/validation N and a P+T method, which are weak tie-breakers here. The evidence gap is modest, hence low confidence.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis). However, PGS004253 is from a disease-focused UC study and provides stronger PRS-relevant evidence via an effect size (OR per SD 1.84, 95% CI 1.76–1.93) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), whereas PGS001855 comes from a UKB-wide portability/framework paper and reports only a modest PRS-comparable metric (partial-r 0.0625) without any AUROC/R2 or effect size. Although PGS001855 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and larger training/validation N, the framework archetype plus weaker performance signal makes it less well-supported than the disease-focused model with strong OR evidence.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported "Cancer of bladder", same method "GWAS Hits" with 13 variants, same EUR-only ancestry, and similarly basic covariates), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R2, which are not decisive). PGS000610 has a trivially higher full-model AUROC/R2, but PGS000611 has clearly stronger effect-size evidence (top 1% vs rest OR 2.66 vs 1.47) and larger training/validation sample sizes, making it slightly better supported overall despite the small AUROC difference.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Ulcerative colitis”) and both are UKB-based framework-style scores with basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). PGS001306 is better supported because it reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.63006 and PGS-only R²=0.02036), enabling direct assessment and a heritability-ceiling sanity check, whereas PGS001855 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625) and no PRS-only AUROC/R², making its predictive strength less directly comparable. Although PGS001855 has more variants (1505 vs 179) and larger training N, those are weaker signals than having explicit PRS-only discrimination/variance-explained evidence.

Both candidates match the target trait (type 2 diabetes mellitus) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model discrimination is not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. PGS002308 is better supported on transportability and PRS signal: it is explicitly trans-ancestry (PRS-CSx) with multi-ancestry GWAS inputs and a very diverse evaluation set (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/GME), and it reports a stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.96) than PGS002243’s HR=1.64, suggesting stronger PRS discrimination. PGS002243 comes from a broad “common diseases across ancestries” framework-style paper with EUR-only GWAS/training (FinnGen) and an incident/time-to-event endpoint (“Incident type 2 diabetes”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch versus the generic T2D target; its reported C-index=0.741 is also a full-model metric and not a clean PRS-only comparator. Overall, PGS002308 has the more disease-focused, cross-ancestry development/validation package and stronger effect-size evidence.

PGS001250 has clearer PRS-comparable performance evidence for urolithiasis: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.5668) and PGS-only R² (0.00592) for a closely aligned endpoint (calculus of kidney and ureter, time-to-event) with only basic covariates. PGS001864 matches the target EFO (urolithiasis) and uses a larger, more genome-wide model (5599 variants) with multi-ancestry evaluation, but it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² and provides only a small partial correlation (0.0323), making its predictive support less directly interpretable. Given both are UKB framework/portability-style scores, the decisive advantage is PGS001250’s cleaner, directly PRS-only metrics on a very similar stone phenotype.

Both candidates are near-identical on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported Bladder cancer; trait_efo urinary bladder carcinoma; phenotyping_reported Cancer of bladder), ancestry (all EUR), cohorts (UKB), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), training size (n=12,992) and validation size (n=13,530), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family signal). Given this near-clone context, PGS000613 has consistently slightly stronger empirical performance/effect evidence than PGS000611: higher full-model AUROC (0.571 vs 0.567), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0125 vs 0.0114), higher top-1% OR (2.91 vs 2.66), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.301 vs 1.284). With no other differentiators, these aligned advantages make PGS000613 better supported.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and use only basic covariates, but PGS001306 is explicitly a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse 179-variant snpnet model—an archetype noted to generalize less well despite having clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (PGS-only AUROC 0.630, R² 0.020, below the h2 ceiling). PGS004253 comes from a disease-focused UC study (immune checkpoint inhibitor-mediated colitis context) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with far broader variant coverage (744,575) plus strong per-SD effect size evidence (OR 1.84), which is a strong PRS signal even though only full-model AUROC (0.66) is reported and PRS-only AUC/R² are missing. Given the framework penalty and sparsity concerns for PGS001306 versus the disease-focused, genome-wide, strong-OR evidence for PGS004253, PGS004253 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 so the full-model AUROC (~0.57) is not a strong differentiator. PGS000613 is better supported by a stronger overall evidence package: larger training sample (12,992 vs 7,469) and substantially larger validation sample (13,530 vs 7,622), and it shows a clearly stronger tail-risk metric (OR top 1% vs rest 2.91 vs 1.47) with a tighter CI, while per-SD OR is similar (1.301 vs 1.292). Given the otherwise minimal differences, the stronger high-risk stratification and broader validation support favor PGS000613.

PGS002075 is the better-supported choice on endpoint fidelity and structural plausibility for generic urolithiasis: its trait_efo is exactly urolithiasis and phenotyping_reported is a direct diagnosis-style “Urinary calculus,” whereas PGS001250 uses a time-to-event phenotype (“TTE calculus of kidney and ureter”), which is a mild mismatch/packaging risk for a generic disease target. Although PGS001250 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.5668; 0.00592) and has a larger validation sample, it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with only 341 variants (snpnet), a pattern that domain guidance flags as less reliable for external performance than genome-wide shrinkage. PGS002075 (LDpred2, 731k variants) is structurally stronger and evaluated across multiple ancestries, but lacks PRS-only AUC/R², making the win lower-confidence.

Both candidates match the target trait (T1D) at trait_reported/trait_efo, but PGS001297 has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.771 and PGS-only R²=0.0912 (no covariates), with basic covariates only, and these are interpretable against the T1D heritability ceiling (well below h2_liability~0.219). In contrast, PGS004874 reports only a full-model time-to-event metric (C-index=0.77) plus HR=2.37, with no PGS-only AUC/R², so its discrimination is not directly comparable and could be covariate/model-structure dependent. Although PGS004874 has a much larger variant count and huge validation N, its training/development sample is very small (n=404; 1000G) and the lack of PRS-only metrics makes support weaker on the visible fields. Therefore PGS001297 is better-supported overall despite being from a pan-trait UKB framework paper.

PGS000738 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS because its publication and framing are vitiligo-focused ("Family Clustering of Autoimmune Vitiligo...") and its evaluation phenotype is at least not explicitly therapy-induced, whereas PGS000760’s phenotyping_reported is "anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients," a clear endpoint mismatch for generic vitiligo risk and a treatment-specific adverse-event context. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS000738 has only a small full-model pseudo R² (0.0386) with unknown covariates, while PGS000760 provides an HR=1.41 but tied to the mismatched endpoint. Given endpoint fidelity is the top criterion and PGS000760 is explicitly off-target, PGS000738 wins despite its imperfect metadata (phenotyping_reported="Red hair").

PGS001795 is the better-supported uterine cancer PRS on PRS-comparable evidence and structural properties: it reports a clean PRS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 (0.001948) in a large EUR evaluation sample (n=170,276) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with very large variant coverage (~912k). Its PRS-only R2 is also below the provided uterine-cancer heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005; liability≈0.0116), making it at least sanity-consistent. In contrast, PGS000541 has good endpoint alignment (malignant neoplasm of uterus) and provides effect sizes (e.g., OR per SD 1.311) but lacks any PRS-only AUC/R2; its reported AUROC (0.576) is a full-model metric and thus not directly comparable, and it is a sparse GWAS-hits score with only 18 variants and much smaller validation (n=6,987).

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Urinary calculus”, trait_efo urolithiasis), publication (same UKB portability paper), training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (n=19,913; same multi-ancestry breakdown). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiators are (i) the available PRS-comparable metric and (ii) structural method/coverage. PGS002075 has higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.0385 vs 0.0323 for PGS001864) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (731,196 vs 5,599), which is generally favored for polygenic traits when other fields are equal. Therefore PGS002075 is better supported than the sparser penalized-regression sibling here.

PGS001536 is endpoint-aligned to vitiligo (trait_reported vitiligo; phenotyping_reported explicitly vitiligo, albeit time-to-event) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), with basic covariates only and a multi-ancestry evaluation set. Its PRS-only R2 is also well below the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs~0.17), supporting metric sanity. In contrast, PGS000760 has a major phenotype mismatch: phenotyping_reported is anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients (therapy-specific, different endpoint), with no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported and only an HR=1.41 in a small validation sample (n=1,584), making it much less directly supported for generic vitiligo risk.

PGS001795 is better-supported for the target trait “uterine cancer” because it matches the umbrella endpoint directly (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: uterine cancer; trait_efo: uterine carcinoma) and, crucially, reports a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R²=0.001948), which is interpretable and below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005; h2_liability≈0.0116). In contrast, PGS003381 targets the dominant subtype (endometrial carcinoma) which is a reasonable proxy but not an exact umbrella match, and it lacks any PRS-only AUC/R²—its only reported metrics are full-model AUROC=0.761 and R²=0.11 with age/PC covariates, which are not comparable as standalone PRS evidence. While PGS003381 has simpler covariates and a coherent cancer-focused endpoint, the absence of PRS-only performance makes its apparent advantage likely covariate-driven and less directly supportive than PGS001795’s explicit PRS-only R².

PGS003381 is better supported for the target “uterine cancer” because its endpoint is the clinically dominant subtype (phenotyping_reported/trait_efo: uterine endometrial carcinoma / endometrial carcinoma), which domain guidance treats as a strong match for uterine cancer, and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant coverage (529,365) versus PGS000541’s sparse GWAS-hits score (18 variants) from a repository-style framework paper. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the higher full-model AUROC for PGS003381 (0.761 vs 0.576) is only weakly comparable, but its covariates are basic (age + PCs) and its much larger evaluation sample (144,479 vs 6,987) adds some support. PGS000541 has exact umbrella-label alignment (uterine cancer) and reports additional metrics/ORs, but its sparse construction and weaker full-model performance make it less compelling overall.

PGS001536 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS: it has coherent endpoint fields (trait_reported vitiligo time-to-event; phenotyping_reported explicitly “TTE vitiligo”) and reports clean PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621) with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and its PRS-only R2 is plausibly below the vitiligo heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS000738 has a major phenotype/metadata mismatch (phenotyping_reported = “Red hair” despite trait_reported vitiligo), lacks PRS-comparable AUROC/R2 (only a pseudo R2 / beta with unknown covariates), and has much smaller validation (n=4,702 vs 67,425). Despite PGS001536 being from a pan-trait UKB framework paper, the explicit vitiligo endpoint alignment plus PRS-only metrics make it clearly stronger than the internally inconsistent PGS000738 record.
